title: AI Is Dead. Organoids Are Alive
gist: A field report on human brain organoids argues the near-term money is in drug screening, not computing: neuropsychiatric drugs fail in human trials about 95 percent of the time, one six-well plate yields up to 4,000 organoids versus five or six research monkeys, and the NIH stopped funding animal-only research in July 2025 while putting $87 million into a Standardized Organoid Modeling Center. Melbourne's Cortical Labs is selling neurons-as-a-service on its CL-1 hardware and aiming to be the Nvidia of neural computing, though despite the headline the text is far more hedged, presenting biological computing as a long-term goal while organoids remain, in the author's words, glorified lab rats.

themes.theme: Drug discovery is the actual near-term business

insights.claim: The human clinical trial failure rate for neuropsychiatric drugs is close to 95 percent, a figure nearly every organoid researcher cites as the core justification for the field.
insights.speaker: Claire L. Evans
insights.so_what: A 95 percent failure rate quantifies the value of any preclinical model that improves human predictivity, sizing the willingness-to-pay for organoid platforms in CNS pharma.
insights.locator: Nearly every organoid researcher I met

insights.claim: Animal testing was never the most physiologically relevant way to validate drugs, only the most practical one, and organoids have changed that calculus by making human-derived tissue the practical option.
insights.speaker: Claire L. Evans
insights.so_what: The substitution argument is economic rather than ethical, which means adoption should track throughput and cost curves, not advocacy pressure.
insights.locator: That’s because drugs are ordinarily tested on animals

insights.claim: One six-well plate can produce up to 4,000 brain organoids, versus a best case of five or six nonhuman primates with implanted electrodes, a throughput gap of roughly three orders of magnitude.
insights.speaker: Claire L. Evans
insights.so_what: Throughput of this magnitude is what makes statistically powered CNS screening feasible for the first time, the single strongest driver of platform demand.
insights.quote: We’re producing, in one six-well plate, up to 4,000 brain organoids.
insights.locator: Think about nonhuman primates, which is the model closest to us

insights.claim: An organoid trained to play Pong is valuable primarily as a test subject for measuring how drugs affect learning and memory, converting a computing demo into a pharmacology assay.
insights.speaker: Claire L. Evans
insights.so_what: Reframes biocomputing demos as instrumentation for drug discovery, which is where near-term revenue is defensible.
insights.locator: In this context, OI isn’t an end as much as it is a means

insights.claim: Because organoids are made from induced pluripotent stem cells taken from consenting adult donors, they avoid both the religious opposition that hit embryonic stem cell research in the 1990s and the animal-rights opposition that constrains lab rats and primates.

insights.so_what: The regulatory vacuum is the field's biggest current advantage and its clearest future discontinuity risk, keyed to organoid size.

insights.claim: Programming living matter carries a failure mode absent from conventional computing: environmental settings such as temperature and oxygen-CO2 mix are user-controllable, and getting them wrong kills the neurons.
insights.speaker: Claire L. Evans
insights.so_what: Irreversible hardware loss from software error is a novel operational and liability risk that has no analogue in cloud computing.

themes.theme: Physical limits and the vascularization bottleneck

insights.claim: Organoids cannot grow much beyond 5 millimeters because without a vascular system to deliver oxygen and remove metabolic waste they develop a necrotic core and suffocate.
insights.speaker: Claire L. Evans
insights.so_what: Vascularization is the single technical gate on organoid scale, so it is the specific capability to track when assessing whether the field's ceiling is about to move.
insights.locator: Conveniently, organoids can’t grow much bigger

insights.claim: Johns Hopkins nanotechnologist David Gracias is developing biomimetic artificial arteries and Annie Kathuria is building rough blood vessel networks from endothelial organoids, work that would remove the 5-millimeter size ceiling.
insights.speaker: Claire L. Evans
insights.so_what: Two independent vascularization approaches at one institution suggests the size ceiling is a near-term engineering problem, which would also reopen the ethics debate.

themes.theme: Culture clash between AI and biology

insights.claim: Silicon Valley treats intelligence functionally, so if an AI does what a conscious human does they will call it consciousness, while biologists who cultivate neural tissue daily refuse the word without heavy caveats.

insights.so_what: The two communities use incompatible evidentiary standards, so claims of machine consciousness should be read as claims about definitions, not findings.
